Buses are usually cheaper and faster to deploy. A city can change routes as neighborhoods grow, add express service, or test demand before making permanent investments. They also work well for lower-density areas. Their weaknesses are reliability and public perception: buses stuck in traffic may be slow unless the city adds bus lanes, signal priority, and frequent service.

Light rail costs much more up front and takes longer to plan, permit, and build. In return, it can carry many riders on busy corridors, attract development near stations, and feel more permanent to residents and employers. It is less flexible, though; if travel patterns shift, tracks cannot easily move.

For accessibility, both systems can be good if stops are designed well, vehicles are frequent, and sidewalks are safe. The practical tradeoff is risk: buses are the better first move when demand is uncertain or budgets are tight; light rail is strongest where a city already has dense, durable corridors that justify a long-term capital bet.
